summary: Describes an XML Schema for IRIS transfer protocols that share common features. It defines common information such as version, supported extensions, and security mechanisms. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A shared form that different lookup systems fill out so they describe themselves in the same way.

questions: internet registry information service xml schema
what is the iris common transfer schema
what does the iris versions element do
how does iris prevent downgrade attacks
subtitle: A shared XML vocabulary that IRIS transfer protocols use to report versions, sizes, authentication results and other status.

tldr.problem: The two IRIS transfer protocols, LWZ and XPC, share negotiation needs: the server must tell clients rich status information that is too complex for simple bit fields and length-specified octet sequences.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4991 defines an XML Schema with five kinds of status information: version, size, authentication success, authentication failure and other.
tldr.outcome: Both transfer protocols can use one schema for capability negotiation. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4991 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2007, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its examples come from the LWZ and XPC transfer protocols, RFC 4993 and RFC 4992.

sections.title: Why a Common Schema
sections.content:
IRIS has two transfer protocols, LWZ (lightweight using compression, RFC 4993) and XPC (XML pipelining with chunks, RFC 4992), that share common negotiation mechanisms. Both need the server to give clients rich status information while negotiating. RFC 4991 defines an XML Schema for it and describes how to use conforming XML.

The RFC gives an example flow. On connection, a server may send version information naming the data models and security mechanisms it supports. A client that recognizes none of the data models may simply close the connection. One that recognizes the data models and a security mechanism may start setting up security before querying.

The schema is formally given in Section 3 of the RFC, and any change to it requires a document that UPDATES or OBSOLETES RFC 4991.
sections.eli5: When you call a help line, the first thing they do is tell you what they can help with. This is a standard way to say that.

sections.title: Version Information
sections.content:
The versions element describes the transfer protocol, the application protocol and the data models. It holds one or more transferProtocol elements, each with zero or more application children, which have zero or more dataModel children. Each has a protocolId and an optional extensionIds attribute.

Both sides are expected to recognize the protocolId of the transfer protocol and at least one application and data model. If that is impossible, an error SHOULD be given and communication ended. Unrecognized extensionIds values MUST be ignored.

The transferProtocol element also has optional authenticationIds, responseSizeOctets and requestSizeOctets attributes, giving the supported authentication mechanisms, the maximum response size the server will give and the maximum request size it will accept. The identifiers have no type and this document defines none, so specifications that use the schema MUST define them. They MUST also describe how octet counts are calculated, because transfer protocols count octets differently.
sections.eli5: The server hands over a short list of the languages it speaks and the locks it can use. The client picks something both know, or leaves politely.

sections.title: Size Information
sections.content:
The size element lets a server say that a request has exceeded a negotiated size (request), or that a response will exceed one (response). Each contains one of two children. exceedsMaximum only says the limit was exceeded. octets also gives a number: the maximum for a request, or the number of octets needed to provide the response.

As with version information, specifications using the schema MUST describe how octets are counted.
sections.eli5: It is a note saying your parcel is too big, and sometimes how big a parcel is allowed to be.

sections.title: Authentication Results
sections.content:
The authenticationSuccess element says a client authenticated successfully, and authenticationFailure says it failed. Both can carry description elements with text that may be shown to a user.

Every description MUST have a language attribute. Clients are not expected to concatenate descriptions, so servers MUST NOT send two descriptions with the same language. A success message can also carry additional security data in a data element of base64 binary type.
sections.eli5: A friendly note that says either you are in or you are not, written in your own language.

sections.title: Other Information
sections.content:
The other element conveys status that may need a human to interpret. It has a required type attribute naming the kind of information. This document defines no identifiers, but intends them to be well known so clients can take different classes of action, so specifications using the schema MUST define them.

It may have zero or more description elements, subject to the same language rules. The RFC's example uses type system with the text "unavailable, come back later". The Internationalization section says XML processors must recognize UTF-8 and UTF-16, and application transfer protocols MUST define any additional encodings they allow.
sections.eli5: It is the catch-all note for any other trouble, like a sign saying the shop is closed, come back later.

sections.title: Downgrade Protection
sections.content:
Transfer protocols that use this schema and offer security such as authentication and confidentiality SHOULD have the server send an initial versions message to the client. That message SHOULD list all relevant authentication identifiers, and its purpose is to help thwart downgrade attacks.

IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iris-transport and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:iris-transport for this document.
sections.eli5: If the server always announces its good locks first, a sneaky person cannot trick you into using a weaker one.
